85.title: The five beloved
85.hook: Daya Ram, Dharam Das, Himmat Rai, Mohkam Chand and Sahib Chand step forward, from different castes and regions
85.howItsDone: At every amrit initiation, five initiated Sikhs serve as the Panj Pyare, and five Sikhs in their place lead nagar kirtan processions at Vaisakhi and other festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vaisakhi, 1699: the Guru's sword, and five who went into the tent. Your line was who will give.

The crowd on the hillside has thinned. Some have run. The ones who stayed are staring at the tent, where five men went in and none came out. Then the flap opens. Out walks the Guru, and behind him, all five. Alive. Dressed alike, tradition says, in fresh saffron-colored clothes and turbans, each carrying a sword, standing tall beside him. A moment ago the crowd was terrified. Now it's looking at five ordinary men who have become something new. The Guru calls them the Panj Pyare.
screen: `THE TENT FLAP OPENS.` → `ALL FIVE, ALIVE.` → `DRESSED ALIKE, BESIDE THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Panj means five, pyare means beloved: the five beloved ones. Now look at who they were, because this is the point. Daya Ram was a shopkeeper from Lahore, in the west. Dharam Das, a farmer from near Delhi. Himmat Rai, a water-carrier from Puri, on the eastern coast. Mohkam Chand, a washerman, or by some accounts a cloth printer, from Dwarka, far away on the western sea. Sahib Chand, a barber from Bidar, in the south. In the society around them, most of these men would never have eaten at the same table. Their castes ranked them high and low. Their homes spanned the subcontinent. And the Guru put them side by side, dressed alike, as one. Then the lovely detail Sikhs point to: their names. Daya means compassion. Dharam, righteousness, doing what's right. Himmat, courage. Mohkam, steadfastness, firmness. And Sahib, sovereignty, a kind of noble dignity. Five names that make a portrait, and Sikhs often say that's what the Khalsa is meant to be. After that day they took new names ending in Singh, and they're remembered as Bhai Daya Singh, Bhai Dharam Singh, Bhai Himmat Singh, Bhai Mohkam Singh and Bhai Sahib Singh. And they're still present. At every Sikh initiation, and at the head of processions, five Sikhs stand in their place as the Panj Pyare. Five beloved, from everywhere, for everyone.

segments.voice: On each breath out, say one name, softly or in your head, and let its meaning come with it: Daya, compassion; Dharam, doing what's right; Himmat, courage; Mohkam, steadfastness; Sahib, dignity. Then go around again, slower, and rest on the one you need most today.
Panj Pyare. The five beloved, the five who answered the Guru's call in 1699, from different castes and regions of India.
Your line: daya, dharam, himmat, mohkam, sahib. Five names that, together, make one portrait. Eighty-five days now.

86.title: Sugar in the iron bowl
86.hook: the Guru stirs water with a double-edged blade while reciting, and tradition says Mata Jito added sugar crystals
86.howItsDone: Sikhs who choose to be initiated take amrit in a ceremony called amrit sanchar, where five initiated Sikhs prepare sweetened water in an iron bowl, stirring it with a khanda while reciting five banis.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Panj Pyare, the five beloved. Your line was daya, dharam, himmat, mohkam, sahib.

Vaisakhi, 1699. The five beloved stand beside the Guru, the crowd watching. He calls for an iron bowl and clean water. He doesn't just pour it. He kneels, takes up a khanda, a double-edged sword, and stirs the water with the blade, round and round, while reciting hymns. It takes a long time. A baby at a font, someone stepping down into a river: water is one way people say something new begins here. And then, tradition says, someone stepped forward and added one more thing.
screen: `AN IRON BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED BLADE.` → `WATER MARKS A BEGINNING.` → `SOMEONE ADDS ONE MORE THING.`

segments.voice: Amrit means the nectar of immortality, literally not-death. You met it inside the name Amritsar, the pool of nectar, on day fifty-five. On Vaisakhi, 1699, amrit took on a new meaning: the sweetened water of Sikh initiation. As Sikh tradition tells it: clean water in an iron bowl, the Guru stirring it with the khanda while reciting five hymns, among them the Japji of Guru Nanak and the Anand, the song of bliss you met on day fifty-three. The bowl is iron, and the blade is steel: strength, courage, readiness. Then the sweetness. Tradition says the Guru's wife, Mata Jito, came with sugar puffs, patashe, and dropped them into the water. Some accounts name Mata Sahib Kaur instead; the sources differ, and Sikhs tell it both ways. Either way, the meaning Sikhs draw from it is the same. The blade alone would make the water hard. The sugar alone would make it soft. Together, strength and sweetness. The Khalsa was to be brave, and also gentle. Firm, and kind. A soldier who serves langar. Then the Guru gave the amrit to the five, sprinkling it on their eyes and hair and giving it to them to drink, all from the same bowl, men of different castes drinking together. That was the point too. The practice continues today as amrit sanchar: five initiated Sikhs, standing as the Panj Pyare, prepare the amrit the same way.

segments.voice: If you can, pour a glass of water, add a little sugar, honey or a slice of fruit, and stir it slowly, watching it dissolve; if not, just picture it. As you stir, think of one place in your life where you've been all strength and no sweetness, or all sweetness and no strength. Then drink slowly, and let the two come together.
Amrit. The nectar of immortality; for Sikhs, the sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, given at initiation.

87.title: The Guru becomes the disciple
87.hook: he asks the five to initiate him too; men take the name Singh and women Kaur
87.carry: wonderful the guru, wonderful the disciple
87.howItsDone: Initiated Sikhs are members of the Khalsa; Sikh men commonly take the name Singh and Sikh women Kaur, and Guru Gobind Singh's receiving amrit from the Panj Pyare is remembered at every Vaisakhi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit: water stirred with a blade and sweetened with sugar. Your line was strength and sweetness.

Vaisakhi, 1699. The Guru has just given amrit to the five beloved. They stand before him, newly initiated. Then he does something unexpected. He kneels in front of them, and asks them to give it to him. A teacher who asks the class to grade her. A coach who runs the same drills as the team. A boss who hands the keys to the newest hire and says: now you lead, and I'll follow. It doesn't happen often.
screen: `THE FIVE, NEWLY INITIATED.` → `THE GURU KNEELS.` → `A TEACHER WHO ASKS TO BE GRADED.`

segments.voice: Khalsa is the word the Guru gave to this new community of the initiated. It comes through Persian from an Arabic root meaning pure, and in the Mughal world it had a precise meaning: land that belonged directly to the ruler, with no middleman in between. So the Khalsa is pure, and it belongs directly to God, with no one standing in the middle. Now watch the Guru. He asks the five to initiate him in exactly the same way, from the same bowl, and he receives the amrit from their hands. He had been Gobind Rai. From that day he was Gobind Singh. The men of the Khalsa took the name Singh, meaning lion. The women took the name Kaur, often explained as princess. A Sikh name no longer told the world your caste or your family's trade. It told them you were a lion, or a princess, in the Guru's family. A Sikh poet remembered as Bhai Gurdas the second later put the moment into a line Sikhs often quote. In plain words: wonderful, wonderful is Gobind Singh, who is himself the Guru and himself the disciple. The one who teaches bows to the ones he has taught. The Guru sets himself inside the community, not above it. Tradition says that day the Khalsa was also given its outward form, the five articles Sikhs keep, starting with uncut hair. That's a story for later in the path. Today is the kneeling.
screen: `KHALSA — PURE, BELONGING TO GOD.` · `THE GURU ASKS THE FIVE FOR AMRIT.` · `SINGH, A LION. KAUR, A PRINCESS.` · `HIMSELF THE GURU, HIMSELF THE DISCIPLE.` · then, large: `WONDERFUL THE GURU, WONDERFUL THE DISCIPLE.`

88.title: Leaving Anandpur
88.hook: after a long siege and broken promises of safe passage, the family is scattered crossing the flooded Sarsa river
88.howItsDone: Each December, Sikhs remember the evacuation of Anandpur and the separation of the Guru's family, with gatherings, recitation and langar at gurdwaras along the route, including Gurdwara Parivar Vichhora on the Sarsa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Khalsa, and the Guru who knelt to his own disciples. Your line was wonderful the guru, wonderful the disciple.

Anandpur, surrounded. The birth of the Khalsa had worried the powerful. The hill rajas around Anandpur saw a growing force on their doorstep that ignored caste and owed them nothing. Over the next few years they fought the Guru, and then they called on the Mughal governors for help. These days of the story are remembered each December, in homes and gurdwaras. They are hard, so this goes a piece at a time. Today, the siege, the promise, and a flooded river on a winter night.
screen: `ANANDPUR SURROUNDED.` → `THE HILL RAJAS AND THE MUGHALS.` → `TOLD EVERY DECEMBER.`

segments.voice: The siege of Anandpur went on for months. Nothing could get in. Food ran out; tradition says the defenders ate leaves and bark. Then the besiegers sent a promise: leave Anandpur, and you'll have safe passage. Tradition says the promise came with sacred oaths, sworn on the holy books of the besiegers' own faiths, and the Guru was deeply doubtful. But his people were starving, and at last, in December, on a bitter night, the whole household and the remaining Sikhs came out and headed south. The promise was broken almost at once. The besieging army attacked the column as it moved. At the Sarsa river, swollen with winter rain, they had to cross in the dark, under attack. Many drowned. Tradition says precious manuscripts, the Guru's writings among them, were swept away. And on that riverbank, the family was scattered. The Guru, with his two elder sons and a small band of Sikhs, went one way. His mother, Mata Gujri, with the two youngest boys, aged about nine and six, was separated and went another, with a family servant. The Guru's wives were led to safety toward Delhi. None of them knew if they would see the others again. Today's line holds onto one thing: scattered is not lost. Each part of the family carried the same faith into the dark. Sikhs have a phrase for the spirit they kept: chardi kala, rising spirits, courage that keeps climbing when everything else is falling.

Hold them there, safely, in your mind, as if you were keeping a light on for them. If you pray, you can pray for them.
Leaving Anandpur. After a long siege and a broken promise of safe passage, the Guru's family was scattered crossing the flooded Sarsa river.
Your line: scattered, not lost. A siege, a broken promise, a river in the dark. Until tomorrow.

89.title: The stand at Chamkaur
89.hook: the Guru's elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, die fighting at Chamkaur, aged about eighteen and fourteen
89.howItsDone: Each December, Sikhs remember the battle of Chamkaur and the elder Sahibzade, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, with gatherings at Gurdwara Katalgarh Sahib and Gurdwara Garhi Sahib in Chamkaur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaving Anandpur, and a family scattered on the banks of the Sarsa. Your line was scattered, not lost.

After the river, the Guru's group was tiny. Tradition says about forty Sikhs, and his two elder sons, Ajit Singh, about eighteen, and Jujhar Singh, about fourteen. They reached a village called Chamkaur, cold, wet and exhausted, and took shelter in a mud-walled house on high ground, more farmhouse than fort. By morning, the pursuing army had surrounded it. Tradition speaks of a vast force against forty. There was no way out. Today, two young men who walked out through the gate.
screen: `FORTY SIKHS AND TWO SONS.` → `A MUD-WALLED HOUSE.` → `SURROUNDED BY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Inside the walls, the Sikhs decided to go out in small groups of five to hold the enemy back, knowing those who went would not come back. Tradition says the elder son, Ajit Singh, asked his father's permission to go. The Guru gave it, helped arm him, and watched from the wall as his son fought and fell. Then the younger one, Jujhar Singh, came to him. Tradition says the Guru asked if he was sure. He was. His father sent him out too, and he fell like his brother. Both of the Guru's elder sons died at Chamkaur, on the same day. Then came something that shows what the Khalsa had become. The Sikhs left inside urged the Guru to escape, so the community would not lose its Guru. He refused. So, tradition says, five of them, speaking as the Panj Pyare, as the Khalsa itself, gave him an order. And the Guru, who had knelt to receive amrit from five of his Sikhs, obeyed the five again. He slipped out in the night. One Sikh, Bhai Sangat Singh, who resembled him, put on the Guru's plumed turban and stayed behind so the enemy would think he was still inside. The Sikhs who stayed died at Chamkaur. Tradition says that among them was Kirpa Singh, the same man who, as Pandit Kirpa Ram, had come from Kashmir to ask Guru Tegh Bahadur for help. Two sons, and a handful of Sikhs, in a mud house. They stood.

90.title: The wall at Sirhind
90.hook: the younger sons Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, nine and six, are executed for refusing to convert; their grandmother Mata Gujri dies too
90.howItsDone: Each December, Sikhs remember the Sahibzade and Mata Gujri during Shaheedi Jor Mela at Fatehgarh Sahib, and many families hold simple gatherings, recitation and langar during that week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stand at Chamkaur: Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, and the five who ordered the Guru to live. Your line was they stood.

On the riverbank, Mata Gujri, the Guru's mother, now an old woman, went one way with her two youngest grandsons, Zorawar Singh, about nine, and Fateh Singh, about six. A family servant offered to hide them in his village. Tradition says he betrayed them for a reward, and they were handed over to the governor of Sirhind, Wazir Khan. It was the middle of winter. This is the hardest story in the camp. Sikhs tell it to their children every December, very gently, and it's told gently here too.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER AND TWO SMALL BOYS.` → `HANDED OVER AT SIRHIND.` → `THE HARDEST STORY IN THE CAMP.`

segments.voice: Sahibzade, a word Sikhs say with enormous love. It means sons of the master, and Sikhs use it for all four of the Guru's sons. Tradition says the grandmother and the boys were kept in a cold tower open to the December wind, the Thanda Burj. Each day the boys were brought before the governor's court and told: accept Islam, and you'll have everything; refuse, and you'll die. Tradition says their grandmother told them stories of their grandfather and great-great-grandfather, the Gurus who gave their lives, and each day the boys walked in and refused. They greeted the court, tradition says, with the Khalsa's own greeting, not a bow. Then someone in that court did something Sikhs have never forgotten. The Nawab of Malerkotla, Sher Muhammad Khan, a Muslim nobleman whose own brother, tradition says, had died fighting the Guru, stood up and protested. You cannot punish children for their father, he said; it is against justice and against Islam itself. He was overruled. Tradition says the boys were bricked into a wall, and then put to death. When Mata Gujri heard, she died in the tower. A merchant named Todar Mal, tradition says, paid for land to cremate the three by covering it with gold coins. Sikhs still honor the town of Malerkotla for the Nawab's protest, and Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib stands at Sirhind. Two boys, nine and six, who would not give up who they were. That is why Sikhs say: the youngest were the bravest.

Sahibzade. The sons of the master, the Guru's four sons; the two youngest, nine and six, died at Sirhind rather than give up their faith.
Your line: the youngest were the bravest. Sikhs carry these names through every December. That's day ninety.

91.title: The forty who came back
91.hook: tradition says forty who had deserted returned with Mai Bhago and died at Khidrana; the Guru tore up their letter of leaving
91.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Chali Mukte, the forty liberated ones, in the Ardas said at the close of worship every day, and each year a gathering at Muktsar in Punjab marks the battle of Khidrana.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sahibzade at Sirhind, who would not give up their faith. Your line was the youngest were the bravest.

I'm out. Don't call me. Leaving the group. A message like that feels final the moment it's sent. Go back to Anandpur, months under siege, food gone, no end in sight. A band of Sikhs from the Majha country near Amritsar can't take any more and want to go home. Tradition says the Guru told them: if you go, write it down. Say you are no longer my Sikhs. Forty of them signed the paper and walked out. At home, nobody welcomed them. And one woman from their own country, Mai Bhago, would not let them rest.
screen: `I'M OUT. DON'T CALL ME.` → `ANANDPUR, UNDER SIEGE.` → `FORTY SIGN A PAPER AND LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Chali Mukte. Chali means forty; mukte, the liberated ones, the freed. It's a strange name for men who deserted, and that's the point. Tradition says Mai Bhago shamed them: if they wouldn't stand with the Guru, she would go herself. She rode out, and the forty rode with her. By then the Guru was on the run through the dry country after Chamkaur, with a Mughal force behind him. They caught up near a pool called Khidrana, around the end of 1705 by the usual dating, and the forty and Mai Bhago stood between the Guru and his pursuers. When the fierce fighting was over, all forty had fallen. Mai Bhago was wounded, and lived. Then the story slows down. The Guru walked the field, the story goes, from man to man, lifting each head, wiping each face, calling each by name. One of them, Mahan Singh, was still breathing. The Guru asked what he wanted. Not a reward. Just this: tear up the paper. The Guru had kept it all this time. He took it out and tore it up. The place was renamed Muktsar, the pool of liberation, and Sikhs still gather there every year. The story doesn't pretend they never left. The paper was real; they signed it. And still the Guru tore it up. Every day, in the Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh worship, the forty are remembered together under that name: not as deserters, but as the ones who came back.
screen: `CHALI MUKTE — THE FORTY FREED.` · `MAI BHAGO RIDES, AND THEY FOLLOW.` · `KHIDRANA: ALL FORTY FALL.` · `THE GURU TEARS UP THE PAPER.` · then, large: `YOU CAN ALWAYS COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who walked away from you, or someone you walked away from: a friend who drifted, a cousin after an argument, maybe a practice or a promise you left behind. Picture the paper, whatever it was, the last text, the slammed door, and see it torn in two; you don't have to fix anything, just let there be a door. If you pray, you can hold them in that prayer.
Chali Mukte. The forty liberated ones, who left and came back. Your week: Panj Pyare, amrit, Khalsa, the river, Chamkaur, the Sahibzade, and now the forty.
Your line: you can always come back. A torn paper, a door held open. See you tomorrow.
